docs.title: Hong Kong relation with Central Authorities
docs.text:
• Central authorities have overall juridiction over the HKSAR (Hong Kong Special Administrative region)

Constitutional basis of HKSAR

  • Both HKSAR and Basic law are derived from the Constitution

  • The Constitution applies to HKSAR

  • The constitution is

  • the fundemental system and task

  • Other laws and system are specific implementation

  • the parent law

  • Other law are branch law formulated in accordance to the Constitution

  • No law or regulation shall be in conflict in the Constitution

  • One country, One constitution, One sovereignty

  • Basic law is formulated in accordance and in compliance with the constitution

Principle of 'One country, two systems'

  • -> Achieve peaceful reunification of the country

  • One country: People's republic of China

  • Two systems: under premise of one country, practise different system

  • One country is the prereqisite and foundation of the two systems

  • When constitutional issues are involved, NPC (national people's congress) and NPCSC(standing commitee of NPC) have the power and responsibility to make desisions

Powers directly excercised by the Central Authorities

  • Establishment of the SAR

  • Deciding on the system to be practised in the SAR

  • Establishment of the governance structure in the SAR

  • Management of foreign affairs relating to the SAR

  • Management of the defence of the SAR

  • Appointment of the Chief Exective and principal officials

  • Archiving and reviewing the legislation of the SAR

  • Amendments to and interpretation of the Basic Law

High degree of autonomy: Central authorities supervise and authorise HKSAR to exercise a high degree of autonomy

Exective power

  • = Power to adminstrate / Formulate the economy, culture, science, education, society, public order, land and resources

  • Should conduct administrative affairs of the region

Legislative power

  • Enact laws on its own on civil, criminal, commercial and litigation matters

  • Through legislative process

  • Has extensive legislative powers

  • Legislature of HKSAR=The Legislative Council

Judicial power + final adjudication

  • Not affected by mainland

  • Established own Court of Final Appeal

Other power

  • Courts can intrepret laws within limits of the Region
  • But if basic law / about relation with the Central Authorities -> seek interpretation from NPCSC via Final Court of Appeal
  • All courts should follow NPCSC interpretation

External affairs

  • Handled by the Central People's congress

  • Allows to conduct relavent external affairs on its own

  • Use 'Hong Kong, China' participate in international activities or organisations not limited to states

  • May use regional flag and regional emblem

docs.title: Political structure of HKSAR
docs.text:
HKSAR is a inseperatable part of the people's republic of China

Relation between Central and local authorities is authorising and being authorised

  • Local authorities have no sovereignty

  • Obtain power from authrisation of the Central authorities

Exective-led system

  • Three powers are accountable to the Central People's Government via the Chief Exective

  • Dual head

  • Head of HKSAR: Accountable to Central People's Government

  • Head of the HKSAR government: Accountable to HKSAR

  • -> Dual accountability

Power and functions

  • Lead the Government

  • Implement laws

  • Sign bills

  • Sign budgets

  • Decide on government policies and issue exective orders

Exective authorities

  • the HKSAR Goverment is the exective authorities of the HKSAR

  • 3 Secretaries of Departments (for Justice, Chief Secretary for Administration, Financial Secretary)

  • 15 Policy bureaux under those

HKSAR power and functions

  • Formulate and implement policies

  • Conduct Administrative affairs

  • Conduct External affairs (authorised by the CPG)

  • Draw and introduce Budgets and Final accounts

  • Draw and introduce Bills (new laws), Motions, and Subordinate legislation (附屬法例)

the Legislative Council

  • is the legislature of HKSAR

  • Government accountance to it

  • Implement laws passed by it

  • Present regular policy adresses it

  • Answer questions raised by its member

  • Obtain approval for taxation and public expenditure

  • Coordinance with the Goverment

  • Exec authorities draft and introduce bills, motions, and budgets -> legislative approves, regulatory document

  • Exective council includes member of Legislative
  • Government officials attend legislative Council meetings to speak on behalf of the Government

The judiciary

  • Independent, free from interference

  • Hears all prosecutions and disputs

  • Members are immunte from legal action

Structure

  • Court of final appeal (Highest, has the power of final adjudication)

  • Can interpret provisions of the Basic Law (except about relation with central authorities)

  • High Court, District Court, ...

docs.title: 1.2 Where does it come from
docs.text:
• Water cycle

  • Water is found mainly in Oceans, Seas, the Atmosphere and the land

  • Water cycles through them through different processes: Water cycle

docs.title: 1.3 freshwater resources globally
docs.text:
• Unevenly distributed

  • Some countries face unstable water supply

  • High rainfall -> enough

  • Lower rainfall -> Water scarcity

docs.title: 1.4 Threads to global freshwater resources
docs.text:
• inadequate freshwater supply

  • Water scarcity affects over 40% of the world population

Why?

Higher demand

  • Population increase

  • -> higher demand for freshwater resources globally for domestic and economic activities

  • Higher living standards

  • Water footprint = the level of development

  • More money -> more meat and diary products -> more water comsumption -> larger water footprints

Decreasing supply

  • Water pollution

  • Toxic or dirty substance e.g. industrial waste or sewage enters lakes, rivers and groundwater4

  • -> Cannot be used

  • Climate change

  • Some region recieve less precipitation -> lower freshwater supply

docs.title: 2 How is it in China
docs.text:
Water problems in China

  • Water Scarcity

  • China has a lot of freshwater But not much per capita

  • -> water may not meet people's needs bc imbalance between water supply and demand

  • Regional and sesonal differences

    • North: less water

    • South: more water

    • Winter: less water

  • Flooding and drought

  • Related to the distribution of precipitation

Location of freshwater resources

  • Most freshwater resources are obtained from rivers and lakes

  • River basin = Area that precipitation flows into river aka drained by a river

  • Most important: Chang Jiang, Zhu Jiang, Heilong Jiang (From most to least)

Wet and Dry regions

  • 32% of land is humid

  • Mainly found in the southern region

  • 53% of land is Semi-arid or arid

  • Mainly found in the nothern and north-western regions

  • South wet, North-western dry

Factors of Percipitation

  • Large part of China has monsoon climates

  • Monsoons = winds that change direction seasonally

  • blowing opposite way in summer and winter

  • Summer

  • Land absorb heat quickily -> air becomes hot and rise -> **air pressure low **

  • Water absorb heat slower than land -> air cooler and sink -> air pressure higher

  • Air moves from high-pressure area to low pressure-area

  • -> blow from sea towards land (southern and eastern part of Asia)

  • Which are onshore winds and summer monsoons

  • carry much moisture -> wet summer

  • Winter

  • Opposite: release heat faster for land / slower for sea

  • Distance from the sea

  • Onshore wind carry moisture

  • Reach inland areas -> moisture lost

  • Eastern coast recieve more percipitation than the inland regions

Relation of percipitation to freshwater resources and water problems

  • Precipitation recieved in a place varies with seasons

  • Area affected by monsoon recieve higher rainfall in summer then in winter

  • Distribution is highly uneven

  • Wet season: higher volume of river flow

  • More water in wet season(summer)

  • water scarcity is more severe in winter

  • Dry season longer then normal -> drought

  • rainfall in the wet season is exceptionally high -> flooding

docs.title: 3 Worsening of water scarcity
docs.text: • bc Increasing demand, Decreasing supply

docs.title: 3.1 Why is demand increasing?
docs.text:
• Increase in population

  • Continuous population growth -> larger demand for water

  • Economic development

  • Since open policy

  • rapid economic growth

  • Economic activities demand for huge amount of water (e.g. manufacturing, agricultural activities)

  • Water is also use ineffectively

    • Only 1/3 of irrigation water is used effectively

    • freshwater resource used to produce one unit of product is way more then more developed countries

  • Rise in living standards

  • Rapid economic development -> income increase -> living standard improve

  • Demand for more food and consumer goods

  • -> more water is needed for different uses

  • Low cost of water

  • Cost of water is low

  • Not enough economic incentive for water users to save water

  • Many people are not aware of the importance of water conservation -> waste water

docs.title: 3.2 Water supply decrease
docs.text:
Water pollution

  • Rapid population growth + economic development -> higher use of water resoruces

  • -> increase in the discharge in sewage (doubled from 1980 to 2015)

  • If sewage is discharged into lakes and rivers w/o treatment -> water pollution

  • Some farmers apply too much chemical (pesticides, fertilizers)

  • Excess chemicals + untreated animal waste may be washed into rivers and lakes by rainfall

  • -> cause water pollution

  • + pollute groundwater

Depletion of Groundwater

  • Water stored underground

  • From water that seep into the ground

  • Major source of freshwater supply if lakes and river are not enough -> dig wells

  • Nothern China

  • freshwater resources are not enough to meet the demand for water

  • People rely on groundwater

  • natural groundwater recharge is small

  • Overdrawing groundwater will reduce groundwater storage

  • -> further decrease freshwater supply

  • Avalibility is a security issue -> must have a secure water supply

docs.title: 4.1 What is it
docs.text:
• Rainfall in an area is much lower then normal for a long period of time

  • A natural hazard

  • (if a area is always dry its arid)

docs.title: 4.2 Impacts of drought in China
docs.text:
On people

  • Farming

  • Lack of water for irrigation / pastures

  • -> Crop faliure, livestock die, farm production drops -> food shortages

  • Industry: Lack of water for processing + cooling: Industrial production will decline

  • Power generation: Water level drop -> hydroelectric power (HEP) production drop

  • Transport: Water transport will be disrupted

  • Daily domestic use

  • Not enough water to use

  • May need to carry out water rationing(restrict water supply)

  • Will cause inconvenience and affect people's health

On environment

  • Lakes and rivers dry up -> Cut-off of river

  • X vegatiation -> topsoil blown away -> **soil erosion **

  • -> intensify desertification (makes land unproductive)

  • -> Sandstorm will be more common

  • plants and animals die -> ecosystem adversely affected

docs.title: 4.3 Where does drought usually occur
docs.text:
• X western part

  • Mainly found in the nothern and southern part of China

docs.title: 4.4 Causes of drought
docs.text:
Physical factors (environmental)

Variation in rainfall

  • Drought is related to rainfall variability

  • Large part of china is affected by monsoon

  • Timing and strength vary between years

  • Wet summer monsoon come late / dry winter monsoon come early

  • Weak summer monsoon: carry less moisture

High temperature

  • Higher temperature -> higher evaporation rates

Human factors

Human induced climate change

  • human activilies emit Green House Gases into the atmosphere

  • -> climate change

  • -> rainfall in China decreasing

High water consumption

  • Water cannot meet the demand even in normal years

  • -> Overdrawing of groundwater

  • Water recieved is below normal -> water avalible is even less -> Drought intensified

Reduced water supply

  • Water wastage and water pollution

  • -> decrease in freshwater supply

  • -> intensifies drought

docs.title: 5.1 China's effort
docs.text:
Increasing supply

  • Building dams and resivoris

  • Wet season: reservoirs behind the dams can store rainwater and river water

  • Dry season: Water released to provide a reliable and adequate source of freshwater use

  • Controlling water pollution

  • Clean up polluted water and lakes: Pass laws and provide money

  • Treat sewage before discharge: Improve sewage management + build new sewage treatment works

  • Reduce discharge

    • Close polluting factories

    • Educate the public

    • Raise water charges

    • Control use of chemicals

    • reuse wastewater

    • purify sewage to recycled water

  • -> More water is drinkable in China

Reducing demand

  • Save water on farms

  • Adopt drip irrigation

  • Use plastic films to reduce evaporation of soil water

  • Prevent water leakage

  • Grow drought-resistant crops (peanuts, sweet potatos, millet, sorghum)

  • Reducing industrial and domestic water useage

  • Adopt water-saving technology in industrial production

  • Pass law to shut down factories that don't comply with water-saving regulations

  • Educate people

  • Increase water charges

docs.title: 5.2 Large scale water transfer project
docs.text:
• South-North water transfer project

  • Advantages

  • Provide reliable and clean water resources -> support industrial development

  • Maintain wetland + river ecosystem

  • Disadvantages

  • People have to be relocated

  • Less water for Hydroelectric power generation

  • Less water flowing downstream -> Natural habitat of fish downstream is destroyed

  • High construction cost (260M RMB)

docs.title: 6 Problem of flooding
docs.text:
6.1 What is flooding

  • Rainfall heavy -> river full -> river water flow over bank -> spread onto surrounding land

  • -> flooding

6.2 Impacts of flooding

  • Injury and loss of life

  • Crop faliure

  • Damaging buildings and infastructure (e.g. roads, buildings)

  • Disrupting transport services

  • Disrupting utility services (gas, electricity supplies)

  • Polluting drinking water

  • Spreading diseases

6.3 Area prone to flooding

  • Eastern and southern parts

  • Coastal areas

  • Where major river basins are found

docs.title: 6.4 Causes of flooding
docs.text:
• More water in a river than it can hold -> flooding

  • Factors

  • Amount of river flow

  • Holding capacity of river (shallow -> less capacity)

Physical factors

  • Heavy rainfall and typhoons

  • Summer monsoons or typhoons bring heavy rain -> + river flow

  • Climate change -> more extreme weather events (typhoons, rainstorms)

  • Low relief + Silting

  • West: Highland

  • East: Coast

  • Rivers in the east flow on gentle slopes

  • -> river flow slows down

  • -> silting (sand and soil is deposited on the river bed)

  • -> reduced holding capacity

Human factors

  • Deforestation

  • Cut tree -> soil easily washed away -> silting + more overland flow

  • Farming practises

  • Overgrazing: Gaze a large amount of livestock

    • -> grass does not have time to recover

  • Over-cultivation: Grow crops intensively on slopes

    • -> Soil becomes poor

  • Cause soil erosion -> + silting

  • Reclaiming lakes (pond)

  • Lakes can store water -> regulate flow

  • Reclaiming (for fish ponds, farming, settlement) -> reduced size of lakes

  • Urban development

  • Cover land with concrete -> rain cannot infiltrate -> overland flow

  • Sewer and drain helps divert rainwater quickly

  • -> Reach river in a shorter amount of time -> flooding

docs.title: 7.1 Ways of easing problem
docs.text:
Regulating river flow

  • Build dams and reservoirs

  • -> hold and store excess river water -> regulate river flow downstream

  • Restoring storagae function of lakes

  • Prohibit reclamation of land

  • Gived up farmlands and fish ponds that is reclaimed

  • Afforestation

  • Increase infiltration

  • Reduce overland flow -> less rapid water into rivers

Increasing holding capacity

  • Preventing silting

  • Reduce soil eurosion

  • Plant trees + control deforestation

  • Terracing(梯田) -> prevent soil eurosion

  • Stopping grazing

  • Building dykes(堤防)

  • Raised height of river banks -> prevent water from overflowing

  • Deepening and widening river channels

  • Allows a larger amount of water within the channels

  • Dredging river channels

  • Remove sediemnts -> lower river bed

docs.title: 7.2 Large-scale flood control project
docs.text:
e.g. Three Gorges Dam (Sanxia) Project -> Control flooding in Chang Jiang basin

Benifits

  • Store water from upstream areas -> lower risk of flooding

  • Provide cheap HEP (hydroelectricity power) -> relieve air pollution

  • Promote tourism

Disavantages

  • Flood large areas of farmland and historicate sites

  • People had to relocate

  • Less fertile soil and less fish -> livelihood of farmers and fishermen is affected

  • Dam collapses -> Serious flooding

  • High construction + maintanance cost

  • Expensive to relocate affected people

  • Harm to environment

  • Sediments trapped -> Reduce soil fertility downstream

  • Fish cannot migrate -> decreased fish species -> affects biodiversity

  • flooded natural habitat of land based wildlife

    • dissolve harmful minerals -> harm

docs.title: Industrial Revolution
docs.text: [[Renaissance]] [[Scientific revolution]] - Technological advancement from 18th to 19th centuries - Key stage of the rise of modern Europe Characteristics - ==Mechanization==: Invented and used many new machines - ==Industrialization==: Experienced rapid growth and replaced traditional agriculture - ==Urbanization==: People moved from countryside to industrial towns Causes - ==Rise in population==: Increase demand for goods, provided labour - ==World trade==: to meet global demand - Accumulation of ==capital==: Invested on new machines + technological innovations - ==Development of science==: Applied technologies to improve industrial technologies Why start in Britain? - Rich in ==natural resources== (e.g. coal, iron) - Had many ==overseas colonies== - ==Enclosure movement==: Farmers lost their land -> move to cities and worked in factories - Government support - ==patent law== to protect rights of inventors - sponsored the ==Royal Society== to carry out scientific experiments Major developments - ==Textile industry== was first - Invention of ==steam engine== -> Spread to heavy industries (iron, steel making) - Made Britain rich - Spread to other European countries - Textile industry - Machine was operated by workers in factories - =='domestic system'== -> =='factory system'== - Spread to other sectors - Sources of energy - ==Steam power== - Watt improved the steam engine - ==Coal gas== - powering machines, gas lighting and cooking - ==Electricity== - 1870s Edison invented light bulb and first electric power system - ==Oil== - discovered in 19th century - used to power machine - Became the primary energy source - Other industries - Coal mining - Used steam power -> improved efficiency - Iron making - Before industrial revolution: Preferred cast iron bc cheap - Reduced cost of wrought iron and steel -> common industrial materials - Improvement in transportation - Before: Poor roads, used ox-cars, horse carts and sailing ships - Land transportation - ==Macadam road== - Better drainage - Smooth surface - 1883: First ==car== - Invented ==steam locomotives== and build ==railways== -> '==Age of railways==' - Became two major means of land transport - Sea transportation - ==Canals== were built - Invented and improved ==steamships== - Carry more further and faster - Communication - Before: by post and takes a long time - Invented ==telegraph==, ==Morse code== and telephone - Built ==telephone networks== - Medicine - Hygiene bad in slums - Started to study social medicines - Vaccines against ==smallpox==, ==cholera== and ==rabies== were invented - Discovered ==X-rays== and ==radium==: ==treat cancer== and observe bodies - Antiseptic surgery was used: prevent septicaemia by bacteria Impacts - Rise of ==capitalism== - Capitalists owned ==means of production== (machines, mines) - Put property into ==production== - Expanded through ==factory system== and ==joint-stock companies== - -> modern capitalism (or industrial capitalism) - Factory system - built factories, installed machines - Employed many workers - -> factory system - ==Division of labour== - Separated into specialized parts - More skilful in preforming their job - Save time and improve quality of work - Joint-stock companies - High cost -> joint-stock companies - Issued ==Stocks== and ==Bonds== to raise capital - Profit was distributed according to investment - Growth of industrial towns - Farmers want to get higher wages -> move to industrial towns - Large number of industrial town in Britain - + Urbanization - Rise of new social classes - ==Capitalist class== - industrialists, businessmen, owners of factories and mines - Rich - Can influence government policies - ==Middle class== - lawyers, doctors and engineers - ==Professional knowledge, expertise -> Wealth== - not as rich and influential - ==Working class== - ==Worked for capitalists== and earned little - Also called '==Proletariat==' - Labour problem - Low income: Woman and children had to work to earn extra - Long working hour: 14-15 hour per day - Frequent accidents: few factories or mines had safety measures - Poor living conditions: - Workers lived in crowded slums - Poor living + sanitary -> diseases - Labour movements - ==Trade Union==: improve ==conditions and wages== - British recognised the legal status (1824) - Trade unions organised '==Chartist Movement==' to demand - shorter working hours and higher wages - Right to vote for every man over 21 - Representative to take part in government - Government passed acts to improve workers' conditions - Disallow Children and woman to work - Limit working hours - But other country didn't improve until 20th century - ==Socialism== - Origin - thinkers criticized ills of capitalism - Private ownership -> few capitalists control means of production - ==Exploit working class for profit== - Means of production should be ==owned publicly== - ==Wealth== should be ==distributed evenly== - -> 'Socialism' - Development - Representatives: British Owen's, French Saint-Simon's, 'utopian socialism', German Engels', Marx's 'communism' - Socialism spread to many countries - Marxism gained the greatest attention - Communist theories and movements affected the world - ==Expansion== of world trade - Western industrial powers imported large quantities of raw materials from different places - Improvement of transportation -> rapid development of international trade and technological exchange - Economic and colonial expansion - Industrial revolution -> more power - -> Acquire more raw materials and overseas markets - Speed up economic and colonial expansion in Asia and Africa - -> New imperialism (extending power through colonization) - Set up many colonies - International economic system developed - Colonial disputes and competition -> conflicts among western powers - -> ==tense international situation==

docs.title: Scientific revolution
docs.text: [[Renaissance]] Entering a new ==age of reason== - New understandings and views about nature, society and the world -> Scientific revolution and the Enlightenment - Modern times = age of faith: people accepted teaching of the Church - Renaissance: people challenged traditional teachings of the Church - Age of reason: scientist explained natural phenomena + proposed different nature laws

docs.title: The Enlightenment
docs.text: [[Renaissance]] [[Scientific revolution]] - A intellectual and cultural movement between the mid-17th and 18th centuries - Stated that people enjoyed ==natural rights== (equality, liberty) - opposed political and social inequalities Causes - Change of value: Promoted idea of humanism -> applied to social and political aspects - ==Discontent with absolutism== - Absolute rulers promoted the '==divine rights of kings==' - -> Europeans began to criticize absolutism Ideas - ==Laws of nature== - Enjoyed inborn rights of equality and liberty - States and government were set up to protect - ==Social contract== - About people and government - ==Locke== + ==Rousseau== suggested - power of government came from people - if government breaks contract and cannot protect people natural rights - people have the right to overthrow - ==Separation of powers== - Montesquieu suggested - ==legislature==, ==executive== and ==judiciary== - prevent absolute rule - ==Constitution + Reforms== - Voltaire suggested - Limit the power of kings and protect people's rights (freedom of speech, press, religion) Spread - academic journals became popular and was a important mean for Europeans to absorb Enlightenment ideas - Publishers were eager to translate and print -> idea became ==widespread== Impact - ==Liberating== minds of European: Awakened Europeans to political system and pursuit to liberty - ==Spread== in Europe and Americans -> American Revolution + French Revolution - Enlightenment ideas -> Absolute rulers gave more rights (Enlightened despots)

Microscopes

  • Light microscopes

  • Light passes through specimen (can see some internel structurs)

  • Max 1600x

  • Coloured image

  • Living specimens can be observed, prepared easily

  • Transmission electron microscopes

  • Electron beam pass through a very thin slice of a specimen

  • 150 000 000x

  • Black and White two-dimensional showing internal structures

  • Scanning electron microscopes

  • Electron beam scan over the surface

  • 200 000x

  • Black and white three-dimensional showing ONLY the external structures

  • Magnification and resolution (clearer, more details) is higher

  • Cannot observe live specimen

Light microscope

  • Compound microscope: eyepiece and objective

  • Eyepiece: magnifying lens

  • Body tube

  • Nosepiece: Choose the objective required

  • Objective: Magnifying lens pointing to the specimen

  • Condenser: Focus light onto specimen

  • Diaphragm: Adjust amount of light

  • Light source

  • Arm: Carry microscope

  • Coarse adjustment knob: Get rough focus

  • Fine adjustment knob: Get sharp focus

  • Stage

  • Base: supports microscope

  • Light penetrates the specimen, enters the objective, passes through eyepiece and enters our eye

  • Image is inverted

Magnification

  • $\text {Total magnification} = \text {Magnification of eyepiece} \times \text {Magnification of objective}$

  • Low-power magnification: Larger area, Fewer details, Brighter

  • High-power magnification: Smaller area, More details, Dimmer

Scientific method

  1. Making observations

  2. Asking a question

docs.text:
Keeping our body healthy

  • Healthy lifestyle

  • Prevention of diseases

  • Eating different kinds of food in the right amount and proportions

  • Enough physical activity

  • Enough sleep and rest

  • Staying away from harmful substances (e.g. cigarettes, alcohol, drugs)

Chemicals of life

  • Inorganic (e.g. Water, inorganic ions) and organic (contains carbon, large)

Inorganic ions

  • Nitrate: source of nitrogen, synthesis of protein

  • Magnesium

  • In animal: Activates some enzymes

  • In plant: Component of chlorophyll, activates some enzymes

Food substances

  • Carbohydrates

  • Lipids

  • Proteins

  • Minerals

  • Vitamins

  • Dietary fibre

  • Water

  • Functions

  • Providing energy (-> Keep body warm)

    • Includes Carbohydrates, Lipids, Proteins

  • Supplying raw materials -> Growth and repair of damaged tissues

  • Maintaining health and normal function

Carbohydrates

  • Made up of Carbon (C), Hydrogen (H), Oxygen (O) atoms

  • H:O ratio = 2:1

  • Monosaccharide

  • Simplest form of carbohydrate

  • Glucose, Fructose: Fruits and honey

  • Galactose: Milk and diary products

  • Disaccharides

  • 2 x Monosaccharide molecules $$ \xrightleftharpoons[\text{Hydrolysis}]{\text{Condensation}}$$ Disaccharide

  • Maltose: 2 x glucose (Germinating barley)

  • Sucrose: glucose + fructose (Sugar cane, sugar beet, table sugar)

  • Lactose: glucose + galactose (Milk and diary products)

  • Polysaccharides

  • Condensation of many monosaccharide

  • Do not taste sweet, insoluble in water

  • Starch: Storage form in plant

  • Glycogen: Storage form in animals

  • Cellulose: Component of plant cell walls (A source of dietary fibre -> cannot be digested)

  • Functions

  • Energy source

  • Starch converted into glucose -> respiration to release energy

  • Converted into glycogen (stored in liver and skeletal muscles) / lipids -> stored as energy reserves

  • As a source of dietary fibre

Lipids

  • Fats Oils Solid Liquid (at room temp) Mainly animals Mainly plants Butter, lard Peanut oil, corn oil

  • Made up of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen atoms

  • H:O ratio >> 2:1 (e.g. 10:1)

  • Insoluble in water (soluble in organic solvents)

  • e.g. Triglycerides (1 x glycerol + 3 x fatty acids $$ \xrightleftharpoons[\text{Hydrolysis}]{\text{Condensation}}$$ Triglyceride + 3 $H_2O$)

  • Classified into fats and oils

  • Functions

  • Energy reserves: Stored in adipose tissues under the skin as subcutaneous fat or around internal organs

  • -> Shock absorber to protect internal organs

  • Heat insulator (subcutaneous fat): Reduces heat loss from body

  • Transportation, absorption and storage of lipid-soluble vitamins

  • Produce some hormones

  • Component of cell membranes

docs.title: Safety rules
docs.text:
Safety rules e.g.

  • Do not work without supervision of teacher

  • Follow strictly the instructions given by the teacher

  • Clean up all spillages at once

  • Clean up the bench after experiemnts

  • Understand the hazards

  • Wear eye protection

  • Turn off Bunsen burner immediately or turn to a small luminous flame

  • Be careful of shooting out of hot liquids during heating

  • Handle corrosive liquids only with tongs

  • Pour acid into a large amount of water with constant stirring

  • Do not eat or drink

  • Wash hands before leaving

Hazard Warning Labels

  • Explosive (e.g. potassium / sodium turned yellow)

  • Oxidizing (e.g. Concentrated sulpuric / nitric acid)

  • Flammable (e.g. alcohol, hydrogen)

  • Carcinogenic (Cause cancer, e.g. Benzene, tetrachloromethane)

  • Toxic (e.g. Chlorine, Bromine, cyanides)

  • Harmful (e.g. iodine)

  • Corrosive (e.g. concentrated mineral acids)

  • Irritant (e.g. Dilute mineral acids)

  • Orders

  • Flammable < oxidizing < explosive

  • Harmful < toxic

  • Irritant < corrosive

Storage of Chemicals

  • Prevent contact of air -> Under paraffin oil

  • Mercury covered with paraffin oil -> Prevent evaporation (vapour highly toxic)

  • Flammable / Volatile -> Stored in a cool place away from direct sunlight or heat sources

  • Absorb moisture (e.g. NaOH) -> well sealed containers

  • Decompose in presence of light -> Brown bottles

  • Sodium hydroxide -> Rubber stopper (glass stopper stucks in the bottle neck)

docs.title: Separating mixtures
docs.text:
• Separate into pure state before they become useful

  • Solutes dissolves in solvent -> Solution

  • Dilute solution, concentrated solution: relatively small / large amount of solute in a given amount of solvent

  • saturated solution: Dissolved the maximum amount of solute it can

Methods of separation

  • Solid + liquid

  • insoluble: Filtration

    • -> Residue (remain on filter paper) + filtrate (collects in beaker)

  • dissolved:

    • Evaporation: -> Increases concentration

    • Crystalization

  • Liquid + liquid

  • Solvent and solute from solution: Distillation

  • Two miscible liquids: Fractional distillation

  • Two immiscible liquids: Separating funnel

Crystalization

  • By cooling hot concentrated solution

  • Water is boiled away before

  • Crystals formed on glass rod on cooling -> Saturated

  • Concentrated solution cools -> Crystals

  • By evaporating solution at room temperature

  • Solvent evaporate -> concentrated and saturated -> Crystalization

  • By slow evaporation / cooling -> Large and well formed

  • Can be seperated by filtration, taken out with spatula and dried by pressing between filter papers

Simple distillation

  • Separate liquid and non-volatile (not easily evaporated) solid

  • Hot vapour formed condense back to liquid on cold surface -> distillate

  • Add anti-bumping granules to prevent pumping due to overheating (may splash out)

  • Water should be passed from the bottom for a better cooling effect

Fractional distillation

  • To separate miscible liquids that boiling points are not too close
  • Fractionating column is packed with glass beads
  • -> Larger surface area for condensation and vaporzation
  • e.g. Separating ethanol and water
  • Vapour contains more ethanol because ethanol is more volatile
  • Vapour condenses when it touches the cold glass beads in the fractionating column
  • Continuous rise of hot vapour -> condensed vapour boils again
  • As vapour rises, it contains more and more ethanol
  • Vapour escapes consists of almost pure ethanol
  • Temperature is measured by a thermometer
  • Remains steady then rises quickily then remains steady: At first the escaping vapour contains almost pure ethanol -> Recorded boiling point of ethanol
  • Different in boiling points should $>10\degree C$

Separating funnel

  • to separate immiscible liquids

  • Mixture place in, shaken and allowed to settle

  • -> Two layers, less dense one on top

  • Remove stopper, open tap, and two liquid will run out in turns and collected in separate containers

docs.text:
Conflicts among European powers

Extreme nationalism

  • Expand aggressively -> Enhance status and influence at any cost

  • Intensified disputes

  • e.g.

  • Germany ('Pan-Germanism') <-> France (Recapture Alsace-Lorraine, Avenge defeat in Franco-Prussian War)

  • Austria-Hungary (Suppress national independence, expand territory) <-> Russia and Serbia ('Pan-Slavism', establish 'Greater Serbia' in Balkan Penisula)

Alliance system

  • Triple Alliance (Central powers)

  • Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy (1882)

  • To isolate France

  • Triple Entente (Allied powers)

  • France, Britain, Russia (1907)

  • -> Divided into two rival camps, Turn into large-scale wars with chain reaction of Allies' intervention

Scrambling for colonies

  • -> Conflicts

  • Incident Power Description Tunisian Incident France, Italy French occupied Tunisia, Italy protested Fashoda Incident Britain, France In Sudan, divided their sphere of influence Moroccan Crises ... ...

Armaments racer

  • Strong military force could safeguard national security and interests

  • Introduced conscription to expand armies -> Increased military expenditures

  • Developed new weapons of mass destruction (e.g. machine guns)

  • Built "Dreadnoughts" (large warships) mainly Britain and Germany

  • -> Reluctant to make concessions in case of conflicts

Pre-war Crises

First Moroccan Crisis (1905-1906)

  • Kaiser William II visited Morocco and declared its sovereign independence

  • -> Discontent with France

  • Forced to make a concession: Recognise French privileges in Morocco at last

Second Moroccan Crisis (1911)

  • France sent troops to Morocco to put down riots

  • Germany sent gunboats to Agadir

  • -> Morocco became a French protectorate

-> Relation between Germany and France worsened

Bosnian Crisis (1908)

  • Ottoman Empire was in decline

  • -> Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina

  • Serbia and Russia wanted to expand -> Finally gave in bc Austria-Hungary was supported by Germany

  • Serbs form a anti-Austrian organisation -> assassination in Sarajevo

Two Balkan Wars

  • Ottoman Empire lost a large part of European territory

  • Austria-Hungary wanted to stop Serbia from expanding

  • -> Supported Albania's independence

  • -> Prevented Serbia from gaining access to the sea

  • -> Straining relationship

  • First Balkan War

  • Balkan League (Serbia, Bulgaria, Montenegro, Greece) VS Ottoman Empire

  • Balkan states seized the European territories of the Ottoman Empire

  • Second Balkan War

  • Balkan League - Bulgaria, Ottoman Empire, Romania VS Bulgaria

  • Bulgaria was dissatisfied with the distribution of land after the war -> Bulgaria was defeated

docs.title: Outbreak of the First World War
docs.text:
The Sarajevo incident (1914)

  • Archduke Franz Ferdinand (heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary) were assassinated during a visit to Sarajevo

  • Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia (23 July)

  • Prohibit all anti-Austrian organisations

  • Remove all officials not accepted by the Austro-Hungarian EMpire

  • Allow Austro-Hungarian officials to enter Serbia

    • to suppress anti-Austro-Hungarian activities

    • to investigate the assassination

    • -> Serbia refused to accept

    • -> Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia (28 July)

docs.title: Paris peace conference
docs.text:
Objectives

  • Re-establish international Order

  • Maintain lasting peace

The Big Three

  • Georges Clemenceau (French Prime Minister)

  • Witnessed two invasions of France by Germany -> Hated Germany

  • Called "the Tiger"

  • Germany should be severely punished so it could no longer threaten France

  • David Lloyd George (Britain Prime Minister)

  • Weaken Germany -> No longer threaten British supremacy

  • Sought a balance -> Affect British trade and allow France to become too powerful

  • Woodrow Wilson (American President)

  • Fourteen Points

    • National self-determination

    • Establish a international organisation for keeping peace

  • Advocated a moderate peace settlement

Treaty of Versailles

  • Punishing Germany severely

  • Surrender all colonies

  • Cede >10% territory

  • Pay reparations of 6.6 Billions

  • Accept all war guilt

  • Army Greatly reduced in size and almost completely disarmed

  • Establishing and international organisation to keep peace

  • Rearranging European territories according to the principle of national self-determination

Impacts

  • Arousing Resentments

  • Germany

    • Defeated countries could not participate in peace conference -> Germans felt treaty was forced upon them

    • Resented Germany needed to accept all war guilt -> strong feeling of revenge

  • Italy: was victorious but didn't get the land promised by Britain and France

  • -> Fascist regimes to lead their countries out of difficult situations

  • League of Nations

  • Geneva, Switzerland

  • Resolve international disputes and promote world peace

  • US refused to join, Germany and Soviet Russia excluded -> limited effectiveness

  • Changing map of Europe

  • Led to the collapse of the four traditional empires (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia, Ottoman Empire)

  • New states were founded on the principle of national self-determination

    • e.g. Poland, Hungary, Yugoslavia
